article_title: Trust in Schools
citation: Bryk, A. S. and Schneider, B. (1988). Trust in Schools: A Core Resource for Improvement. https://www.amazon.com
title: Build and sustain a broad base of trust across a school community as a critical resource when embarking on major school reform
description: The principle follows from the book's central finding: relational trust should be treated as a core resource for improvement, not an intangible afterthought. Bryk and Schneider "show how a broad base of trust across a school community can provide a critical resource as education professional and parents embark on major school reforms," and the book "offer insights into how trust can be built and sustained in school communities." It also "identifies some features of public school systems that can impede such development," so reformers should attend to those impediments while cultivating trust.
requirements: Requires attention to the social exchanges of daily school life that generate or fail to generate trust
constraints: Features of public school systems can impede the development of trust, as the book identifies
target_learning_goals: Successful implementation of school reform and improved student learning
examples: In the 12 Chicago elementary schools studied, high-trust schools saw educators experiment with new practices and work with parents, alongside marked gains in student learning.
key_sources: Bryk, A. S. and Schneider, B. (1988). Trust in Schools: A Core Resource for Improvement. https://www.amazon.com

article_title: How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School (Expanded Edition)
citation: John D. Bransford, Ann L. Brown, and Rodney R. Cocking, editors, National Research Council. (2000). How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School: Expanded Edition. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/9853
title: Bridge the science of learning to actual classroom practice as a distinct follow-up step
description: The volume treats linking research on learning to practice as a distinct effort requiring its own committee and report. The Preface states that after the original science-of-learning volume, "a second NRC committee, the Committee on Learning Research and Educational Practice, was formed to carry that volume an essential step further by exploring the critical issue of how better to link the findings of research on the science of learning to actual practice in the classroom." The principle is that synthesis of learning science and translation into practice are separate, both necessary steps.
requirements: A body of learning-science findings already synthesized
target_learning_goals: applying learning research to instructional design and classroom practice
examples: The Committee on Learning Research and Educational Practice produced How People Learn: Bridging Research and Practice, published in June 1999, whose material was drawn on for this expanded edition.
key_sources: John D. Bransford, Ann L. Brown, and Rodney R. Cocking, editors, National Research Council. (2000). How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School: Expanded Edition. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/9853

article_title: Teaching the Way Students Learn Best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School
citation: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale
title: Whole-school design pattern combining community vision, inquiry instruction with social-emotional supports, restorative discipline, and a professional community of practice
description: The report identifies a constellation of four mutually reinforcing school-design factors that it argues produced Bronxdale's outcomes: "a compelling vision of students and school as a caring, safe, collaborative community," "the integration of inquiry instruction with social-emotional supports," "educative discipline that puts restorative practices into action," and a faculty committed to "teaching the way that students learn best" while "continuously learning together in a community of practice." The pattern treats culture, pedagogy, discipline, and adult learning as one integrated design rather than isolated programs.
requirements: Structures such as small class size and advisory to build close relationships; distributed leadership; intensive ongoing professional development; and multi-tiered academic, health, and social supports.
constraints: The report notes the school's evolution took about 7 years and that its first year, before these practices were in place, was "in disarray" with fights and an unsafe climate.
target_learners: Diverse high school learners, including students from low-income households and students with disabilities in inclusion settings
target_learning_goals: Self-reliant, independent learning; curiosity; creative problem-solving; agency; academic and emotional self-regulation
examples: Bronxdale implemented advisory, Peer Group Connections, restorative circles, peer mediation, youth court, small classes of about 22 students, and a senior capstone project presented to a jury of peers and faculty.

article_title: Longitudinal alterations in brain morphometry mediated the effects of bullying victimization on cognitive development in preadolescents.
citation: Menken Miriam S., Rodriguez Rivera Pedro J., Isaiah Amal, Ernst Thomas, Cloak Christine C., Chang Linda. (2023). Longitudinal alterations in brain morphometry mediated the effects of bullying victimization on cognitive development in preadolescents. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101247
title: Brain morphometry as a partial mediator/suppressor of the effect of bullying victimization on cognitive development
description: The article proposes that structural brain changes in bullying-impacted regions statistically mediate or suppress part of the effect of bullying victimization on cognition. Using LMM-derived bullying-impacted regions, mediation models estimated the indirect effect of bullying on cognitive scores through subcortical volume, cortical volume, surface area, and thickness. The authors report that "Changes in brain morphometry mediate or suppress 7–16% of the effect of bullying on cognition", with fusiform surface area acting as a suppressor and precentral thickness as a partial mediator. The framework follows the AGReMA reporting guideline and a suppression-effect interpretation per MacKinnon et al.
requirements: Longitudinal MRI morphometry and cognitive testing in bullied and matched non-bullied children
Bullying-impacted regions identified first via LMMs before mediation testing
constraints: The mediation model did not allow nesting by scanner, so scanner type was included as a covariate instead
Temporal precedence of bullying before cognitive effects is argued, not experimentally established
target_learners: preadolescent children in the ABCD Study cohort
target_learning_goals: understanding neural mechanisms linking bullying victimization to cognitive outcomes
examples: Mediation analyses showed larger right fusiform surface area suppressed 11.8-15.6% of the bullying effect on crystallized composite and picture vocabulary scores, and thinner precentral cortex mediated 7.0% of the effect on inhibitory control and attention
key_sources: Menken Miriam S., Rodriguez Rivera Pedro J., Isaiah Amal, Ernst Thomas, Cloak Christine C., Chang Linda. (2023). Longitudinal alterations in brain morphometry mediated the effects of bullying victimization on cognitive development in preadolescents. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101247

article_title: Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs
citation: Melissa E. Hudson and David W. Test. (2011). Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs. Research & Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities, 36(1-2), 34-45. http://www.education.uncc.edu/access/
title: Define literacy broadly for students with extensive support needs to include both access to age-appropriate literature and reading independence
description: The review defines literacy as "skills that increased access to age appropriate literature (e.g., listening comprehension) and reading independence (e.g., vocabulary and comprehension), including emergent literary skills." A broad definition matters because students' skills may fall far below peers; a narrow reading-independence definition could leave students stuck "getting ready to read" or deemed unable to benefit. It also emphasizes shifting materials and instruction as students grow older.
requirements: Literacy instruction should include measures of both access skills (e.g., listening comprehension) and reading-independence skills
constraints: If literacy were defined solely as a bridge to reading independence, students with extensive support needs could be deemed unable to benefit from literacy instruction
target_learning_goals: access to age-appropriate literature and reading independence
examples: The review applied this broad definition as an inclusion criterion, requiring at least one literacy dependent variable in reviewed studies
key_sources: Melissa E. Hudson and David W. Test. (2011). Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs. Research & Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities, 36(1-2), 34-45. http://www.education.uncc.edu/access/

article_title: Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally
citation: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x
title: Bridge-building metaphor for adapting instruction across cultures
description: The article proposes bridge-building as a metaphor for how increased cultural sensitivity changes design practice: designers identify gaps between an instructional experience as designed and learners' expectations and capabilities, then bridge those gaps with additional support. Building bridges stimulates "separating deeper principles from particular application," identifying gaps through immersion, learner feedback in up-front analysis, and formative evaluation, allowing design flexibility, and educating other stakeholders. Shawn emphasized attending to "danger points" where learners may unintentionally misunderstand.
requirements: Designers must discover learners' frames of reference and prerequisite knowledge to locate where bridges are needed
constraints: Derived from practitioner interviews in an exploration study; the authors call for research on how to bridge gaps more effectively
target_learning_goals: Making instruction accessible and meaningful across cultural contexts
examples: Rose, developing instruction in Egypt, immersed herself in local environments and used Egyptians' social nature as a bridge toward interaction and team problem solving, also teaching meta-cognitive strategies like brainstorming.
key_sources: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x

article_title: Five-Year-Old Children’s Working Memory Can Be Improved When Children Act On A Transparent Goal Cue
citation: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4
title: Brown-Peterson working memory task with animated goal cue tracking for preschoolers
description: A computerized Brown-Peterson task in which 4- and 5-year-olds memorized series of one to three colored drawings of animals and objects presented visually with their auditory name, then recalled them after a retention interval during which an animated shape moved across the screen. Children tracked the moving shape — an abstract form, an abstract black rectangle cue, or a transparent school-bag cue — either visually or with a finger. Performance was measured by the number of words correctly recalled, with a control condition as baseline for the between-subjects comparison.
requirements: E-Prime 2.0.10 on laptops in a quiet room; two 15-minute sessions with a pause for 4-year-olds; training trials before each session; item names recorded by a male voice and drawings selected to exceed 80% correct denomination at 4 years of age
constraints: Retention intervals differed between age groups (7,800 ms for 4-year-olds, 7,100 ms for 5-year-olds), so the design does not allow direct age comparisons of working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: verbal working memory for picture-item series under a concurrent tracking task
examples: Each child completed a control condition and one of four experimental conditions, with condition order counterbalanced and two experimenters blind to the aim of the experiment
key_sources: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4

article_title: Guiding group cognition in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7
title: Browser plug-in infrastructure for portable cross-platform collaboration scripts
description: The article describes an infrastructure for collaboration scripts that can be ported to different collaboration environments, developed by Christof Wecker and colleagues. It works "by means of a browser plug-in, which can recognize inputs from different CSCL systems and provide responses in accordance with a cross-platform script definition." Its application was illustrated in a realistic educational application setting.
requirements: Motivated by the finding that creation of one-off scripts is time consuming and hard to scale up for widespread classroom usage
target_learners: students and teams working in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: guided collaboration through scripted learning trajectories
examples: The plug-in recognizes inputs from different CSCL systems and responds according to a cross-platform script definition
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7

article_title: Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge
citation: Esther Ziegler, Dragan Trninic, Manu Kapur. (2021). Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge. Instructional Science 49, 313–336. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09544-7
title: Sequence brief problem-solving attempts before instruction when teaching multi-step algebraic procedures
description: The article recommends starting with micro productive failure occasions: have students generate a single solution attempt to a procedural problem before the relevant principle is formally taught, repeating this cycle for each new principle. The article reports this minimal intervention "impacted the development of algebraic procedural knowledge," with a stable advantage on isomorphic problems at both delays, and states that the unstable conceptual-measure interaction "does not change our recommendation of starting with micro productive failure occasions."
requirements: Failure occasions must be followed by formal instruction on the relevant principle
Students must be prompted to generate a solution even when they claim not to know how to solve the problem
constraints: The intervention showed no effects on conceptual explanation or transfer measures in this study
Caution is warranted before classroom application because procedural fluency without conceptual understanding is of limited value
examples: In the study, PS-I students processed problem-solving sheets before receiving instruction in the subsequent worksheet, while I-PS students processed identical sheets after instruction as additional practice
key_sources: Esther Ziegler, Dragan Trninic, Manu Kapur. (2021). Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge. Instructional Science 49, 313–336. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09544-7

article_title: Better beware: comparing metacognition for phishing and legitimate emails
citation: Casey Inez Canfield & Baruch Fischhoff & Alex Davis. (2019). Better beware: comparing metacognition for phishing and legitimate emails. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09197-5
title: Brier-score decomposition into calibration, resolution, and knowledge as metrics of detection metacognition
description: The article uses probability judgments to reveal metacognitive states of mind, scoring them with the Brier score, which "can be decomposed into three components, calibration (or reliability), resolution, and knowledge (or uncertainty)." Calibration measures whether confidence judgments correspond to relative frequencies; resolution measures the variance of correct answers associated with different probability judgments, so high-resolution individuals "are better able to discriminate between correct and incorrect judgments by assigning them different probabilities." Judgments are binned into six confidence ranges (50–59% through 100%), with lower calibration scores and higher resolution scores indicating better metacognition; knowledge, capturing outcome uncertainty, is excluded as not an element of metacognition.
requirements: Confidence judgments elicited on a probability scale (here 50%–100%) for each detection decision, so they can be binned and scored against observed outcomes
constraints: Knowledge is not an element of metacognition and is not considered further by the article
Scores are computed per individual over a fixed set of items (N = 38 forecasts per person here)
target_learners: adults judging email legitimacy (crowdsourced adults and community-dwelling students and retirees)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of one's own deception-detection accuracy in digital literacy tasks
examples: Applied to 40-email detection tasks in two experiments, scored separately for 19 phishing and 19 legitimate emails
key_sources: Casey Inez Canfield & Baruch Fischhoff & Alex Davis. (2019). Better beware: comparing metacognition for phishing and legitimate emails. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09197-5

article_title: Gender Disparity in Computational Thinking Pedagogy and Assessment: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Suya Liu · Yun Dai · Oi Lam Ng · Zhihui Cai. (2025). Gender Disparity in Computational Thinking Pedagogy and Assessment: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10095-3
title: Brennan and Resnick's three-dimensional CT framework (concepts, practices, perspectives) as the study's organizing scaffold
description: The article adopts Brennan and Resnick (2012)'s framework as its theoretical scaffold for understanding CT learning and assessment. It classifies CT into three dimensions: "concepts, practices, and perspectives" — concepts are foundational programming ideas (sequences, loops, conditionals, events), practices are how learners apply concepts in problem-solving (testing, debugging, decomposition), and perspectives address how learners view themselves in relation to computing. The framework integrates cognitive, procedural, and dispositional dimensions and directly informed the coding of the learning-outcome moderator.
requirements: Assessment tools must be aligned with the specific CT dimension being measured for the framework to support meaningful synthesis of evaluation results
constraints: The meta-analysis is constrained to male/female comparisons because most quantitative primary studies report only binary gender data
target_learning_goals: computational thinking concepts, practices, and perspectives
examples: The coding scheme classified learning outcomes as CT performance, self-perceived CT skill, or CT attitude, mapped onto the framework's three dimensions
key_sources: Suya Liu · Yun Dai · Oi Lam Ng · Zhihui Cai. (2025). Gender Disparity in Computational Thinking Pedagogy and Assessment: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10095-3

article_title: The Brilliance–Belonging Model: How Cultural Beliefs About Intellectual Ability Undermine Educational Equity
citation: Christina A. Bauer, Aashna Poddar, Eddie Brummelman, & Andrei Cimpian. (2025). The Brilliance–Belonging Model: How Cultural Beliefs About Intellectual Ability Undermine Educational Equity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10034-2
title: The Brilliance–Belonging Model: brilliance-oriented FABs and brilliance stereotypes undermine belonging through self-related and other-related pathways
description: The Brilliance–Belonging Model is a theoretical framework proposing that brilliance-oriented FABs (beliefs that a field requires exceptional intellectual ability) and brilliance stereotypes (associations of brilliance with certain groups) jointly reduce educational equity. As the article states, "students from groups targeted by negative brilliance stereotypes are perceived—by themselves and others—as not belonging in contexts where brilliance-oriented FABs are common." These perceptions compromise psychological safety and invite disempowering treatment, producing gaps in achievement and representation. The model specifies a self-related pathway (self- and meta-perceptions of low belonging lowering safety, self-efficacy, and motivation) and an other-related pathway (others' low-belonging perceptions producing bias), which mutually reinforce each other in a self-perpetuating cycle.
requirements: Both belief types must operate jointly: a field perceived to require brilliance and brilliance stereotypically associated with certain groups
constraints: The model remains agnostic on whether exceptional intellectual ability is actually necessary for success in any given context
The model remains agnostic about the nature of brilliance itself (fixed vs. malleable, universal vs. non-universal)
target_learners: students from groups facing negative brilliance stereotypes: women, people from lower-SES backgrounds, and people from historically marginalized racial/ethnic groups
target_learning_goals: sustained sense of belonging in academic contexts
equitable achievement and representation across academic fields
key_sources: Christina A. Bauer, Aashna Poddar, Eddie Brummelman, & Andrei Cimpian. (2025). The Brilliance–Belonging Model: How Cultural Beliefs About Intellectual Ability Undermine Educational Equity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10034-2

article_title: Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7
title: True causal hypotheses should survive testing with a broad set of different analyses; model-choice-sensitive support warrants suspended judgement
description: The authors report that the RI-CLPM and the LCSM (with a covariance between X at time T and subsequent change in X), as well as corresponding multilevel models fitted to person-mean centered scores, reached the same conclusion when applied to data with a known causal effect by construction. They argue that if support for a hypothesis is sensitive to specific modeling choices, as the REM appears to be, the hypothesis should probably not be seen as corroborated.
requirements: Access to a broad set of alternative statistical analyses applicable to the same longitudinal data
constraints: The article's robustness demonstration rests on data with a known causal effect by construction (adding stones in a container on the weight of the container), not on the self-concept data itself
target_learners: educational researchers evaluating causal claims from panel data
target_learning_goals: judging when cross-lagged findings corroborate a causal hypothesis
examples: Sorjonen & Melin (2024) tested RI-CLPM, LCSM, and multilevel models on container-weight data with a known causal effect

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Jere Brophy
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x
title: Brophy and Good's chapter in the Third Handbook of Research on Teaching — the definitive archival summary of process-outcome research, 1973–1983
description: Rosenshine's tribute identifies the chapter by Jere and Tom Good in the Third Handbook of Research on Teaching as containing a summary of each process-outcome study Brophy and colleagues conducted. examples: Rosenshine states the chapter summarizes each of the process-outcome studies Brophy and his colleagues conducted

article_title: Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic
citation: Kennedy, A. I., Mejía-Rodríguez, A. M., Strietholt, R. (2026). Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic. Preprint submitted to Learning and Instruction. https://github.com/OxCGRT/covid-policy-dataset
title: Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory as a framework for civic education outcomes
description: The article uses Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory to frame how civic education outcomes are shaped beyond formal schooling. It states the theory "provides a valuable framework for understanding civic education, emphasizing how an individual's development is shaped by interactions across multiple environments". The model nests microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, and chronosystem around the individual student, with the chronosystem capturing historical events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors use it to justify hypothesizing that lockdown measures influenced civic knowledge, trust, and expected participation through home, parental, societal, and event-related layers.
requirements: Civic learning is understood as occurring across multiple nested environments, not only within educational institutions
constraints: The article applies the framework to grade 8 students' civic outcomes in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic
examples: The authors hypothesize that students confined to the microsystem of their home may have developed decreased trust in institutions and increased propensity for protest, shaped by parents, significant adults, and media

article_title: Exploring young learners’ prompted and unprompted SRL think-alouds
citation: Rebecca Pape, Joachim Thomas. (2026). Exploring young learners’ prompted and unprompted SRL think-alouds. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102294. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102294
title: Brainix metacognitive prompt set (set goal, prioritize, reflect prompts and calendar goals planner)
description: A set of metacognitive prompts embedded in the Brainix CBLE for lower secondary students, based on Zimmerman’s (2000) and Winne and Hadwin’s (1998) SRL models. The set comprises "three prompts, the set goal prompt, the prioritize prompt, the reflect prompt, and the calendar goals planner"; prompts were presented at the beginning and end of the learning unit, with the calendar available throughout. All prompts are adaptive to students’ progress and visualize learning goals with a progress bar and goal icons.
requirements: Prompts were created using the Design Thinking approach and piloted with ten 6th graders before the study
constraints: The specific context of the learning environment, learning materials, and metacognitive prompting limits the generalizability of the present findings
target_learning_goals: metacognitive SRL activities including goal setting, strategic planning, and reflection
examples: In the study, prompts were presented at the beginning and the end of a 30-min English learning unit in Brainix

article_title: An fMRI study on the generalization of motor learning after brain actuated supernumerary robot training
citation: Yuan Liu, Shuaifei Huang, Weiguo Xu, Zhuang Wang & Dong Ming. (2024). An fMRI study on the generalization of motor learning after brain actuated supernumerary robot training. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00294-y
title: Brain-machine-body account: BCI-SRF training enhances motor sequence learning generalization through functional reorganization of the sensorimotor network
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that motor sequence learning depends on the sensorimotor network, and that "BCI-SRF training enhances the generalization ability of motor sequence learning through functional reorganization of sensorimotor networks". Three properties are proposed: novel limb morphology activating broader sensorimotor neural resources, efferent and afferent pathways via EEG decoding and FES sensory feedback enhancing cortical-subcortical interactions, and sixth-finger motor imagery recruiting additional frontal resources. The framework integrates the frontal-parietal circuit and the SM_cortex-cerebellar-thalamus cortical-subcortical circuit as jointly supporting motor sequence learning.
requirements: Brain-actuated SRF system with EEG decoding of sixth-finger motor imagery and TENS sensory feedback forming an extra SRF control circuit
Sustained longitudinal training (20 sessions over 4 weeks in this study)
constraints: The authors state their data are insufficient to elucidate the exact role of each circuit effect or their combination
No direct evidence of structural plasticity effects was provided; functional plasticity was the observed basis
Sample size was not very large, and clinical patients have not yet been tested
target_learners: Healthy adults learning human-machine interaction skills
Potentially stroke patients needing motor relearning (speculated application)
target_learning_goals: Generalization of motor sequence learning to novel sequences
Functional reorganization of the sensorimotor network supporting skill acquisition
examples: Twenty healthy right-handed participants were randomly assigned to BCI-SRF or inborn finger training for 20 sessions over 4 weeks, with novel SRF-finger opposition sequences measured at pre, post, and 1-month follow-up

article_title: Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence
citation: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w
title: Nonlinear mixed-effects Bayesian regression model of WM trajectory components
description: A fully disaggregated nonlinear Bayesian mixed-effects model, implemented in the R package brms, estimating each participant's initial accuracy, rate of change (a time constant), and asymptotic accuracy as a continuous function of trial number, with an exponential change curve bounded via logistic-regression link functions. Fixed effects of task order and feedback were included and found not reliable on their own. The authors state it "prevents the conﬂation of components of learning inherent in many other forms of learning estimates".

citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: A synthesized set of brain-compatible learning principles for instructional design
description: The dissertation synthesises principles reported across multiple authors (Fogarty, Jensen, Materna, Sousa, Craig, Smilkstein, Caine and Caine) into a summary table, noting that "Currently, no single authoritative list or taxonomy exists that describes and encompasses all known brain-compatible learning principles". constraints: Some principles (e.g. healthy lifestyle, unique brains) are difficult for an instructional designer to control for in a blended or classroom environment

description: The Brain Based Teaching Approach is grounded in Caine and Caine's Brain Based Learning Principles and implemented through three instructional methods. The article defines them: "Orchestrated Immersion - makes a learning setting that fully engages students in many learning skills", "Relaxed Alertness - removes fear in the learners while preserving highly stimulating settings", and "Active Processing - lets the learner combine and assume material by actively practicing it". title: Deliver brief manualized interventions through typically trained school mental health providers to overcome the research-to-practice gap
description: The article argues that evidence-based interventions can reach real-world students when designed for school delivery: brief (16 sessions under 20 minutes), manualized, implemented during the school day with only two parent meetings, and delivered by "typically trained school mental health providers" without ongoing supervision. In this trial, providers received only the manuals and two 1-hour review meetings, yet implemented both interventions with fidelity and produced significant improvements. description: The article demonstrates that a single 40-minute session of mental rotation practice using an object completion task — children "see two parts of a flat shape and then point to one of four pictures that shows the shape as a whole" — improved calculation performance in 6- to 8-year-olds. It offers an existence proof that spatial training per se can improve math, supporting instructional exploration of spatial cognition in early math.

No general improvement in spatial ability on the PMA Spatial Relations subtest

title: Brief, blended upskilling programs can build primary care capacity to deliver pulmonary rehabilitation without post-graduate qualifications
description: The article supports workforce development as a strategy for expanding access to pulmonary rehabilitation by upskilling existing primary care clinicians. The program combined a 6–8 hour self-directed online module with a 4-hour small-group practical workshop, with competency thresholds on knowledge and observed practical skills. The authors conclude that "a short training course can improve knowledge and skills of physiotherapists and AEPs to provide PR, without the need for formal post-graduate training", potentially enabling scalable delivery in primary care.
requirements: Practices need at least two staff members, adequate space for group exercise, a 10-meter straight track for a field walking test, and accessibility for people with chronic respiratory disease.

target_learning_goals: Pulmonary rehabilitation program establishment and delivery
examples: 17 clinicians (8 physiotherapists, 9 AEPs) completed the LFA online training program and a 4-hour practical face-to-face module delivered by PR experts, with direct observation of the six-minute walk test, incremental shuttle walk test, and 1-minute sit-to-stand test against a pre-defined competency checklist.

description: The intervention pattern consists of "three monthly 50-min education sessions" delivered in the ICU setting, with content covering "MDRO definitions, transmission routes, national IPC guidelines, proper isolation techniques and outbreak case reviews". Delivery used "lecture-based presentations, visual aids and brief scenario-based discussions", with sessions offered twice daily to accommodate rotating shifts. Attendance is mandatory and facilitated by infection control staff with advanced IPC training

title: Use relatively short quizzes to support college student success at a favorable cost-to-benefit ratio
description: The article's instructor-facing recommendation is that instructors can support student success with relatively short quizzes rather than longer ones. constraints: The authors caution that the study included a small sample from one upper-level psychology course, and additional research is needed to clarify the number of questions needed to produce improvements
target_learning_goals: exam performance and desirable academic behaviors such as participation and studying
examples: The course administered 5-point quizzes: five questions drawn randomly from each chapter's Practice Quiz in the 5Q condition and all ten in the 10Q condition, with answer keys displayed and reviewed in class.

title: Bronfenbrenner's socio-ecological model as the study's framework, restricted to micro- and meso-level systems
description: The study adopts Bronfenbrenner's socio-ecological model, which "divides these patterns of interaction into a system of four levels i.e. micro-level systems, meso-level systems, exo-level systems and macro-level systems". The micro level covers home, neighbourhood and school; the meso level covers interactions between micro systems such as parents and teachers. The authors use it to frame parenting style (a micro-level factor) and family SES as determinants of academic performance, and state that "the current study focused only on these two levels" — micro and meso — due to their direct influence and resource constraints.
requirements: Analysis must be restricted to factors at the micro level (e.g., parenting style, family) and meso level of the model that directly influence children's learning and performance
constraints: Exo-level and macro-level systems are excluded; the article states the study was "limited to only two levels, Micro- and Meso-levels" due to time and financial constraints
target_learners: Secondary school students (classes 9 and 10, ages 15–18) in government and private schools in District Malakand, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
target_learning_goals: Understanding how family-level factors (parenting style, socioeconomic status) relate to children's academic performance
examples: The study measured parenting style via Robinson et al.'s scale with authoritative, authoritarian and permissive subscales, and family SES via a modified Kuppuswamy scale, framed as micro-level factors in the model

citation: Vieira Lais Meirelles Nicoliello, Camargos Paulo Augusto Moreira, Ibiapina Cássio da Cunha. (2022). Bronchoscopy simulation training in the post-pandemic world. Jornal Brasileiro de Pneumologia. https://doi.org/10.36416/1806-3756/e20210361
title: Taxonomy of bronchoscopy simulators by fidelity: wet lab, low-fidelity, and high-fidelity virtual simulators
description: The review organizes bronchoscopy simulators into three classes. Animal-model training is "known as a wet lab simulation"; low-fidelity simulation uses inanimate airway models into which real bronchoscopes are inserted, from non-anatomical labyrinths to silicone mannequins; and "High-fidelity simulation is based on the use of computers for virtual projection of the airways, also known as virtual simulators." Each class trades off realism, cost, ethics, and equipment risk, and the review traces their development from the 1999 swine model and PreOp Endoscopic Simulator onward.
requirements: High-fidelity virtual simulators require computer hardware and software for virtual projection of the airways
Low-fidelity and 3D-printed models require a real bronchoscope, which can be damaged
constraints: Even the most up-to-date virtual models reproduce tactile sensitivity only in a rudimentary way
Low-fidelity models do not simulate resistance to scope or breathing movements and are not very realistic in anatomy
Pediatric simulators are absent or of limited availability
examples: Named models include the Laerdal Airway Management Trainer and Airway Larry (low-fidelity), the AccuTouch Endoscopy Simulator and Gi-Bronch Mentor (high-fidelity), and 3D-printed models costing USD 5.00 to USD 100.00

title: Breakout rooms with a dedicated instructor at a 1:4 ratio for supervised skills practice
description: The session pattern moves students from a whole-group demonstration into small virtual breakout rooms where each group has a dedicated instructor who supervises practice, 'pins' student screens to observe individuals, and gives real-time feedback. target_learning_goals: Supervised acquisition of procedural and surgical skills with individualised feedback
examples: Students watched a pre-recorded reef-knot video, then practised in breakout rooms under direct supervision, cycling through slip knots, suturing and trabeculectomy releasable suture tying.
